source.title_on_document: Do Conversational Interfaces Limit Creativity? Exploring Visual Graph Systems for Creative Writing

supplement.where: No supplementary material or appendix is identified. Code and additional system documentation are linked at https://github.com/abhinavsood2002/Chaining-GenAI-for-Ideation (p. 1, footnote 1; pp. 4-5, system and task descriptions).
supplement.holds: The repository is described as containing system code, the topological-sorting algorithm, interface images, and task templates; it was not read, and the paper does not identify outcome statistics held only there.

paper_design_summary: Eight convenience-sampled volunteers participated in an online, within-person comparison of graph-based and conversational generative-AI interfaces, writing character descriptions or world settings with task variants across interfaces (pp. 4-5, User Study and Study Design). Half received each interface first, but the mechanism for allocating that order is not stated, so the study is coded other rather than as a confirmed randomized or non-randomized design (p. 4, Study Design). Analyses concern questionnaire ratings and qualitative feedback about the systems, including a full analysis with P4 and an alternative excluding P4; example writing is reproduced but its creativity or diversity is not scored (pp. 5-7, Post-study questionnaire, Results, Tables 1-2, and Example Task Answers from P3).

studies.label: Online user study comparing graph-based and conversational interfaces

assignment.what_was_assigned: Interface order: graph-based first or conversational first, with half of participants in each order; participants used variants of the same creative-writing task across the two interfaces. The text does not state how participants were allocated to orders, tasks, or variants.
assignment.quote: To address the first confounding variable, half of the participants were given the graph-based system first, while the other half were given the conversational system first.
assignment.locator: p. 4, Study Design, final paragraph; p. 4, User Study, describes each participant being asked to use both systems.

arms.name: Graph-based system
arms.description: Graph interface for chaining generative models, with editable task-specific templates. This is a within-person condition sharing the same participants as chat; the full questionnaire analysis includes P4, who was unable to use the graph system (pp. 4-5, Study Design; p. 6, Table 1 and Results).

arms.name: Conversational system
arms.description: Chat interface using the same language model and system prompt as the graph interface, with image generation and example queries. This is the comparison condition for the same participants; counts refer to the full questionnaire analysis with P4 included (p. 4, Baseline and Additional Changes; p. 6, Table 1 and Results).

participants.who: Convenience sample recruited through creative-writing social media groups and acquaintances, including people who did not engage in creative writing, amateur writers, and a professional writer. The analyzed count is the full questionnaire sample including P4, who could not use the graph interface; Table 1 also gives an analysis with all of P4's responses removed from both conditions.
participants.quote: The most significant limitation of our study is the limited number of participants (8) in our user study.
participants.locator: p. 7, Limitations (quoted sample count); p. 4, User Study (recruitment and paired procedure); p. 6, Participant Demographics, Table 1, and Results (full sample and analysis excluding P4).

ai_tool.how_used: Participants prompted a language model through connected graph nodes or a conversational interface; both used the same language model and system prompt and could generate images. The graph condition supplied editable task-specific templates (p. 4, Baseline and Additional Changes; p. 5, Study Design continuation).

task.description: Write brief character descriptions or world-setting descriptions, using different variants of the same task across systems: protagonist versus antagonist, or rainforest versus arctic community. Participants drafted answers in an interface notepad (pp. 4-5, Baseline and Additional Changes and Study Design).
task.duration: Approximately 1:30-2 hours per participant to complete the tasks (p. 4, User Study).

eligibility.reason: The order of the two generative-AI interfaces was balanced across participants, but random assignment or a specifically non-random allocation mechanism is not stated (p. 4, Study Design); convenience sampling describes recruitment, not condition assignment. Only 8 people were analyzed in the full questionnaire sample, below the 50-person threshold, and both conditions use the same people (p. 4, User Study; p. 6, Participant Demographics and Table 1; p. 7, Limitations). Outcomes are self-reported satisfaction, perceived influence on the task answer, ease of use, collaboration, and qualitative feedback; no creativity or diversity measure is scored on the produced writing (pp. 5-7, Post-study questionnaire, Results, Tables 1-2, and Example Task Answers from P3). The outcomes array is empty because there are no qualifying output-scored outcomes. This is an excluded system/user study, with no qualifying observational or AI-versus-human output context evidence.

one_line_finding: Among 8 participants, some reported that the graph interface aided ideation, but its mean ease-of-use rating was 2.875 versus 4.125 for chat with P4 included (higher means easier); no output creativity or diversity was scored (p. 5, footnote 4; p. 6, Table 1 and Results; p. 7, Table 2 and Limitations).
